title: Māori GIS
description: Explore iwi-led mapping, whenua and land information, Māori place names, cultural heritage, environmental planning, data sovereignty and the communities who developed practical Māori GIS in Aotearoa.

sections.title: Whenua, maps and authority
paragraphs: Long before GIS, Māori geographic knowledge was held through whakapapa, oral histories, journeys, place names, maps and relationships with whenua and wai. Survey and land-court records introduced a different administrative record, important for understanding the history of land interests but not interchangeable with iwi or hapū knowledge. The history of Māori GIS includes how mapping was used to document land loss and claims, as well as how Māori organisations subsequently built and governed their own spatial information.

The Māori Land Information System was being digitised by April 2002. On 4 March 2011 the Māori Land Court launched its GIS Project, allowing users to view, search and download geographic information about Māori land blocks, including an interface available in te reo Māori. It drew on LINZ data and Google mapping technology; the published launch is evidence of the service at that date, not proof that every underlying ownership or boundary question was resolved.

sections.title: Iwi-led GIS
paragraphs: A 28 June 1996 Wellington conference on Mapping Māori Land and Resource Aspirations provides an early dated marker for GIS-related debate over whenua. In November 2003, the Motueka Iwi Resource Management Advisory Komiti (MIRMAK) began an iwi-led GIS information project involving Te Tau Ihu iwi and Manaaki Whenua research support. Its documented purposes included environmental management, consenting, planning and cultural records.

The Motueka work drew a distinction between environmental information suitable for broader exchange and cultural information requiring restricted access. That distinction remains important: availability of public maps and government datasets does not imply permission to publish iwi-held knowledge, wāhi tapu locations or other sensitive material.

By November 2004 the independent Crown Forestry Rental Trust was publicly describing the use of 3D maps to assist Māori claimants and the Waitangi Tribunal. A later Tribunal bibliography lists multiple thematic inquiry map books commissioned in 2005, including maps supporting Central North Island and Te Urewera hearings. The 2006 Whanganui ArcFlax edition adds a further, separately documented form of delivery through an interactive GIS DVD. The dates and format of each are established by different records; their shared programme context does not identify the software or full dataset content used to produce every map.

A documented example of distribution by physical media is the Crown Forestry Rental Trust's ArcFlax Edition 2.0 Whanganui (2006). The National Library records an interactive GIS DVD credited to Duane Wilkins and requiring ArcReader 9.1. The record establishes the edition and the means of access, without giving a full inventory of its GIS layers or the date of any earlier edition. This work belongs alongside iwi-led information systems as an example of how GIS was made usable for Treaty research.

The Te Paparahi o Te Raki inquiry register adds a particularly useful archival detail. Its January 2007 entry A045 describes ArcFlax 1.0 Northland as a two- and three-dimensional GIS viewer supplied on five discs, with Crown-purchase, Old Land Claims and Native Land Court mapping among its contents. This is a different regional product from the Whanganui Edition 2.0 DVD catalogued in 2006, so the numbers alone cannot determine their development order. The preserved record documents the Northland package's map categories; access to the actual discs is still needed to examine the GIS layers, interfaces and source files.

sections.title: Place names and heritage
paragraphs: Ngāi Tahu's Kā Huru Manu Cultural Mapping Project built a research-led geospatial record of names, routes and places. A 2005 Kāi Tahu ki Otago pilot and mapping hui from 2007 preceded the public atlas launched in 2017. The project linked archival work, community review and a place-name information system to digital mapping; the public atlas contains material approved for release, not the full iwi knowledge base.

The distinction between public interpretation and iwi-controlled source material is as important to the history as the software. GIS and digital archives can help reconnect places with narratives, but context, accuracy and mana whenua decisions govern how such information is represented.

sections.title: Practitioners and wānanga
paragraphs: Māori GIS practitioner conferences in 2009 (Christchurch) and 2010 (Lower Hutt), followed by online practitioner networks, formed part of the move towards peer learning and applied Māori GIS capability. The former Māori GIS Facebook group was later deleted after being hacked; its history should not be mistaken for a current public group.

From October 2020, LINZ reported fortnightly online Ngā Poutama Matawhenua mapping wānanga delivered with Te Kāhui Manu Hōkai and supported by Journey GIS. The programme subsequently continued as monthly sessions covering whenua, mapping tools, historical aerial imagery, coastal information, environmental monitoring and 3D storytelling. The collaboration received the 2021 Community Impact Spatial Excellence Award at the 2022 award ceremony.

sections.title: Data sovereignty
paragraphs: Māori data sovereignty is not simply a software-access question. Te Mana Raraunga, formed in 2015, articulated principles of Māori authority, collective benefit and responsibilities in relation to data. GIS work involving iwi knowledge requires decisions about consent, storage, provenance, access rights, ownership, interpretation and reuse.

The examples in this collection distinguish openly licensed government geospatial datasets from restricted Māori information. They describe public historical evidence and do not reproduce protected whakapapa, wāhi tapu information, unpublished iwi maps or community knowledge that has not been approved for public release.
